idea_angle: A calm guide for parents and teens to financially motivated sextortion: how it starts, why it isn't the victim's fault, why paying doesn't end it, and the exact steps and free tools to use. Posted ahead of Safer Internet Day.

script.title: Sextortion: what every parent and teen should know (and do)
script.hook: 1 conversation with your teen this week could matter more than any app setting. Here's how sextortion works, and what to do.

segments.heading: Why this week
segments.narration: This Tuesday is Safer Internet Day, and this video is about one of the hardest online crimes to talk about: sextortion. Someone, usually a stranger pretending to be a teen, gets a private photo or video, then threatens to send it to friends and family unless they're paid. The FBI says the financially motivated version mostly targets teenage boys. I'll keep this calm and practical: how it starts, why it works, and exactly what to do. If anyone watching is in that situation right now: it's not your fault, and there's a way through.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes sitting beside a parent and a teen No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it starts
segments.narration: It usually starts with a friendly message on a social app or game. The profile looks like someone your age, often attractive, often with mutual friends, because the scammers add lots of people first. The chat is flattering and moves fast. Within hours, sometimes minutes, it turns flirty and they send a photo they say is of themselves. Then they ask for one back. The moment they get it, the tone changes completely: a screenshot of your friends list, and a demand for money.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a chat that turns from hearts to a warning sign No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why it works
segments.narration: It works because of panic. The threat is designed to make you feel like your life is over, and that you have minutes to act. They'll count down. They'll say they'll send it to your school, your coach, your parents. They'll ask for gift cards, payment apps or crypto. And they count on you being too scared to tell anyone. That secrecy is their whole business model. The moment a trusted adult knows, most of their power is gone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a ticking clock and a closed door No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Not your fault
segments.narration: So the first thing to say, and to hear, is this: it's not your fault. These are organized criminal groups who do this to thousands of people as a job, with scripts. Being tricked by a professional isn't stupid, and it isn't something to be ashamed of. Parents, if your kid comes to you, that's the bravest thing they could do. Your first words matter more than anything else. Something like: thank you for telling me, you're not in trouble, we'll handle this together.
segments.on_screen_text: Not your fault. You're not alone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a parent hugging a teen No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Don't pay
segments.narration: Second: don't pay. It feels like paying will make it stop, but the FBI says paying usually leads to more demands, not fewer. Once they know you'll pay, you become a better target. Stop replying. You don't need to explain or argue. But don't delete the account or the messages yet, because they're evidence.
segments.on_screen_text: Don't pay. It doesn't end it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a closed wallet and a muted chat No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The steps
segments.narration: Here are the steps, in order. One, screenshot the profile, the username, the messages and any payment requests. Two, block the account, and report it on the app. Most platforms have a specific option for this. Three, report it to the FBI at tips dot F B I dot gov, or call one eight hundred CALL F B I. Four, if money was already sent, contact the payment app or card company, and keep the receipts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a numbered checklist on a phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Take It Down
segments.narration: If the person in the image is under eighteen, use NCMEC's free tool called Take It Down, at take it down dot n c m e c dot org. It creates a digital fingerprint of the image on your own device, without uploading the image itself, and participating platforms use that to find and remove copies. You can also report to NCMEC's CyberTipline. Adults can use the reporting tools on each platform, and there are services that help with removal too.
segments.on_screen_text: Take It Down: free, for under-18s
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a shield over a photo with a fingerprint No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Talking about it
segments.narration: Parents, don't wait for this to happen. Bring it up casually, maybe by sharing this video. Say: if anyone ever threatens you with a photo, come to me, I promise I won't be angry, and we'll fix it. That one sentence is the most effective protection there is. And for anyone feeling overwhelmed, scared or hopeless right now: call or text nine eight eight, any time, day or night. Please send this to a parent, a teacher or a coach, and follow for calm, practical scam advice.
segments.on_screen_text: 'Come to me. I won't be angry.'

idea_angle: On Valentine's Day: the four ways romance scammers ask for money (the emergency, the favor, the investment, the package), with what each sounds like and how to say no, plus how to help someone who's in one.

script.title: Valentine's Day: the 4 ways romance scammers ask for money
script.hook: 4 ways romance scammers ask for money. Every scam uses at least 1 of them.

segments.heading: Why today
segments.narration: Happy Valentine's Day. Today's a lovely day if you've met someone online, and it's also one of the busiest days of the year for romance scammers, because feelings are running high. The FTC says romance scams are among the costliest scams per person. And they all, eventually, ask for money in one of four ways. If you know the four, you can spot a scam early, for yourself or for someone you love.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding a heart and a magnifier No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. The emergency
segments.narration: Ask number one, the emergency. 'I've been in an accident.' 'My daughter's in hospital.' 'My account's frozen and the hotel is going to throw me out.' It's urgent, it's emotional, and it's always somewhere far away. The giveaway is that a real person in a real emergency has other options: family, friends, their bank, their embassy. Somebody you've never met in person shouldn't be their only lifeline.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an ambulance light glowing over a phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. The favor
segments.narration: Ask number two, the favor. Smaller, and it often comes first, as a test. 'Can you grab me a couple of gift cards?' 'Can you receive a payment for me and send it on?' 'I need two thousand five hundred for leave papers to come see you.' The gift cards are always a scam, the FTC is clear on that. Receiving and forwarding money can make you a money mule, without knowing it. And soldiers don't pay for leave.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a small gift card and a forwarding arrow No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. The investment
segments.narration: Ask number three, the investment. This one doesn't feel like a request at all. 'My uncle taught me crypto trading, let me show you.' They help you open an account on an app or website, and your balance grows, fast. Then they suggest you put in more, maybe your savings, to 'build our future'. When you try to withdraw, there's a tax or a fee. The profits were never real, and the platform is part of the scam.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a chart going up on a fake app No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. The package
segments.narration: Ask number four, the package. 'I've sent you a gift,' or 'I've shipped my savings to you for safekeeping.' Then a courier emails: held at customs, pay a fee. Then insurance. Then a certificate. There's no package, and the courier is the same person. Real carriers don't take customs fees by wire, gift card or crypto to an individual.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a box with a customs stamp No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Saying no
segments.narration: So how do you say no, if you really like this person? You can say it kindly: 'I don't send money to anyone I haven't met in person. Let's video chat this week and meet when you're back.' A real partner will understand. A scammer will push, guilt you, get angry, or suddenly have a new emergency. Their reaction is your answer.
segments.on_screen_text: 'I don't send money to anyone I haven't met'
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two chat bubbles, one calm, one angry No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Helping someone
segments.narration: If you think someone you love is in one, don't lead with 'you're being scammed'. They'll defend the person. Instead, ask curious questions. Have you video chatted? Have you met? What did they say when you asked to? Offer to reverse image search the photos together. And say 'I'm on your side' a lot. Shame drives people back to the scammer, who is always kind.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an adult child and parent at a kitchen table No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If money's gone
segments.narration: If money has already been sent, stop sending more. Contact the bank, card company or gift card company right away. Save every message. Report it at report fraud dot F T C dot gov and to the FBI at I C 3 dot gov. And watch out for 'recovery' services that promise to get it back for a fee, which is the next scam. Send this to someone dating online, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: IRS scams 2027: every way scammers fake the IRS, and how the real IRS contacts you
script.hook: 6 ways scammers pretend to be the IRS, and 1 simple habit that beats every one.

segments.heading: Why now
segments.narration: Filing season is in full swing, and so are IRS impersonators. They know you're expecting to hear about taxes, so a message 'from the IRS' doesn't feel strange this time of year. Here are the six ways they pretend to be the IRS, how the real IRS actually reaches people, and where to check anything for yourself. General education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding a tax form and a magnifier No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Phone calls
segments.narration: One, the phone call. It might be a robocall, 'this is your final notice', or a live person with a badge number. They say you owe back taxes, there's a warrant, and you must pay today by gift card, wire, payment app or crypto. The real IRS doesn't threaten to have local police arrest you, and it doesn't demand a specific payment method. The IRS may call in some situations, usually after it's sent letters, but it won't demand immediate payment like that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a badge and a siren No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Texts
segments.narration: Two, the text. 'Your refund is on hold, verify your identity.' 'You're eligible for a tax credit, claim now.' With a link. The IRS says it doesn't start contact with taxpayers by text about refunds or bills. Any text like this is fake. Forward it to seven seven two six, which is the spam reporting number, and report it to the IRS.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a link and a hook No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Emails
segments.narration: Three, the email. These copy the IRS logo, the colors, even the footer. 'A new document is in your account,' or 'final notice, balance due.' They link to a fake sign-in page, or attach a file that installs malware. The IRS doesn't start contact by email about bills or refunds either. Forward fakes to phishing at I R S dot gov, and don't open attachments.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an email with a paperclip and a bug No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake letters
segments.narration: Four, the fake letter. Some scams now come by mail, because people trust paper. A real IRS notice has a notice or letter number, usually in a corner, and it explains your rights and options. Look up that number on the IRS's 'understanding your notice' page. If a letter asks you to pay by gift card, or to call a number that isn't on IRS dot gov, treat it as fake.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two letters side by side, one with a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Social media
segments.narration: Five, social media. Fake IRS accounts reply to posts about taxes, or send messages offering help with your refund. And then there are 'tax hacks' on social media that lead people to claim credits they don't qualify for. The IRS won't message you directly about your account on social media.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a chat bubble with a fake badge No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: At your door
segments.narration: Six, at your door. It's rare, but people do show up claiming to be IRS agents. Real IRS employees who visit carry two forms of official credentials, and you can verify them. They won't demand payment on the spot by gift card or crypto. If you're unsure, don't let them in, and call the IRS on the number from IRS dot gov to check.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a front door with a peephole No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check and pay
segments.narration: So here's the habit that beats all six: go to the source. Sign in to your IRS online account by typing I R S dot gov yourself. That's where you can see balances, notices and payments. If you owe, pay at I R S dot gov slash payments. If you got a letter, look up the notice number. You never need a link, a caller, or a gift card to deal with the IRS.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a laptop with an official account page No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Reporting
segments.narration: Report phone impersonators to TIGTA at tigta dot gov. Forward fake IRS emails to phishing at I R S dot gov, and texts to seven seven two six. If you think someone used your details to file, follow the IRS identity theft steps and get an Identity Protection PIN for next year. Save this video for tax season, send it to whoever does your family's taxes, and follow for one scam decoded every day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes pointing at three report icons No text, no logos, no real people.

idea_angle: For anyone who owes the IRS: what tax relief companies promise, what the FTC warns about, and the free or low-cost official options (payment plans, Offer in Compromise pre-qualifier, Taxpayer Advocate Service, Low Income Taxpayer Clinics).

script.title: Owe the IRS? Free help first, and how to spot a tax relief scam
script.hook: 3 free places to get help with a tax bill, before you pay a relief company thousands.

segments.heading: Why it matters
segments.narration: If you owe the IRS money you can't pay right now, you're not alone, and it's stressful. That stress is exactly what tax relief ads target. Some companies are legitimate. But the FTC warns that others charge large fees and make promises they can't keep. So here's what the ads promise, the red flags, and the official options that are free, or much cheaper, to try first. General education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes sitting at a table with a tax bill No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The promise
segments.narration: The ads usually promise to settle your tax debt for pennies on the dollar, stop wage garnishments, or make penalties disappear. They're on TV, radio and social media, especially in tax season. The truth is that the IRS does sometimes accept less than the full amount, through something called an Offer in Compromise. But it depends on your income, expenses and assets, and many people don't qualify.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a TV ad with a big smile No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Red flags
segments.narration: Red flags, from the FTC: a promise of results before they've looked at your finances. Large fees up front. Pressure to sign today. Being told to stop talking to the IRS. And vague answers about who will actually work on your case. If they can't tell you the name of a CPA, enrolled agent or tax attorney you can look up, be careful.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. five red flags in a row No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payment plans
segments.narration: Now the official options. First, payment plans. Many people can set up a short-term or long-term payment plan with the IRS themselves, online, at I R S dot gov. There can be setup fees, and interest and penalties keep adding up until it's paid, but it stops things getting worse and it's something you can do without hiring anyone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a calendar of small payments No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Offer in Compromise
segments.narration: Second, the Offer in Compromise. That's the 'pay less than you owe' option the ads talk about. The IRS has a free online pre-qualifier tool on its website that tells you whether you're likely to qualify, before you spend anything. If you're not likely to qualify, a company charging thousands to apply probably can't change that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a checklist with a calculator No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free help
segments.narration: Third, free help. The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent part of the IRS that helps people stuck with tax problems, for free. And Low Income Taxpayer Clinics give free or low-cost help to people who qualify, including representation in disputes. You can find both on the IRS website.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an advisor figure with a heart No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you hire
segments.narration: If you do decide to hire help, choose a CPA, enrolled agent or tax attorney you can verify. Get the fees in writing, and know what you're paying for. Never sign anything that stops you from contacting the IRS yourself. And never pay anyone who says the IRS is about to take your house unless you sign today.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a handshake over a written agreement No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wrap up
segments.narration: So: payment plans, the pre-qualifier, and free help first. Then, if you need more, someone you can verify. Save this for anyone who's worried about a tax bill, and follow for more plain-English money and scam advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes giving a thumbs up No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Government imposter scams: Social Security, Medicare, courts and more (Slam the Scam Day)
script.hook: 6 government agencies scammers pretend to be. Here's what each real 1 never does.

segments.heading: Why it works
segments.narration: This week is Slam the Scam Day, run by Social Security's inspector general to fight government imposter scams. These scams work because most of us are a little afraid of getting in trouble with the government. Scammers turn that fear into urgency. Here are six agencies they pretend to be, what the fake call sounds like, and the one thing each real agency never does.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes next to a row of official seals No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Social Security
segments.narration: One, Social Security. 'Your Social Security number has been suspended due to suspicious activity.' Or, 'your number was used in a crime.' Then, move your money to protect it. Social Security numbers don't get suspended. Social Security won't threaten you with arrest, demand immediate payment, or ask for gift cards, wires or crypto. Report fakes at o i g dot s s a dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a Social Security card with a fake lock No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Medicare
segments.narration: Two, Medicare. 'Your card is expiring, confirm your Medicare number.' Or, 'you qualify for a free brace or genetic test.' Medicare cards are free, and Medicare generally won't call to ask for your number. A stolen Medicare number can be used to bill for care that never happened. If in doubt, call one eight hundred MEDICARE.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a health card and a phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Courts
segments.narration: Three, the courts. 'You missed jury duty, there's a warrant, pay a bond now.' Sometimes with a real judge's name. Courts don't call or text to collect fines for missed jury service. Look up the court's number on its official website and call the clerk.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a courthouse and a gavel No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: FTC and safe accounts
segments.narration: Four, the FTC itself, or a 'federal agent'. This is the most dangerous one. 'Your identity has been stolen, your bank accounts are compromised, move your money to a safe account,' or 'withdraw cash and hand it to a courier.' The FTC will never tell you to move money, buy gold, or hand cash to anyone. No real agency will.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. money being carried out of a bank by a shadow No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Utilities
segments.narration: Five, utilities. Not technically government, but they use the same fear. 'Your power will be cut off in thirty minutes.' Real utilities send notices first and don't demand gift cards, crypto or store barcodes. Call the number on your bill.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a light bulb and a ringing phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Police
segments.narration: Six, police or sheriffs. 'There's a warrant, pay to clear it.' Law enforcement doesn't call to collect payments to stop an arrest. Caller ID can be faked to show a real department. Hang up and call the department's non-emergency number yourself.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a badge with a crack No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The family plan
segments.narration: So here's the family plan. One rule: we never pay anyone who calls us, texts us or emails us first. We hang up and call the real number ourselves. Agree on that rule with your parents this week. Practice the line: 'I don't do that on the phone, I'll call you back.' And make sure they know they can always call you first, without feeling silly. Send this to your parents for Slam the Scam Day, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

idea_angle: Spring break and spring travel scams: fake rentals, fake booking and airline support numbers, 'free vacation' calls, and travel deals on social media, with checks for each.

script.title: Spring break scams: fake rentals, fake booking sites and 'free trips'
script.hook: 5 travel scams wait for spring break bookers. Here's how each works, and the 2-minute check for each.

segments.heading: Why spring
segments.narration: Spring break means lots of people booking trips at the same time, often last minute, often on their phones. Scammers love that. Here are five travel scams that peak this time of year, and a quick check for each one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes in sunglasses with a suitcase No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake rentals
segments.narration: One, the fake rental. A beach house or condo, beautiful photos, a price well below everything nearby. The 'host' asks you to book directly and pay by payment app, wire or gift card to save fees. The photos are often copied from a real listing, and the house might belong to someone else. The check: reverse search the photos, map the address, and only pay through the booking platform or by credit card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a beach house made of cardboard No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake booking sites
segments.narration: Two, fake booking sites. Ads and search results for 'cheap flights' or hotel deals can lead to sites that look like real travel sites but take your card and never book anything, or charge hidden fees. The check: book directly with the airline or hotel, or with a travel site you already know, by typing the address. Then confirm the booking on the airline's or hotel's own site.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a website with a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake support numbers
segments.narration: Three, fake support numbers. Your flight is cancelled and you search for the airline's phone number. Some results, including some ads, show numbers that aren't the airline's. The 'agent' charges a rebooking fee, or asks for your card and personal details. The check: use the airline's app, or the number on its official website, typed yourself.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a headset with a warning sign No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: You've won a trip
segments.narration: Four, 'you've won a free trip.' A call, text or letter says you've won a cruise or a resort stay. You just pay taxes or port fees, or attend a sales presentation. Real prizes don't ask you to pay to collect them. If it's a timeshare pitch, you'll know within the first hour.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a gift box with a price tag No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Social media deals
segments.narration: Five, social media deals. 'Selling my spring break package, can't go anymore, half price.' Or a travel account offering deals in comments. Some are hacked friends' accounts. The check: never pay a stranger for a trip transfer, and if it's a friend, call them to confirm it's really them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a social post with a suitcase and a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paying safely
segments.narration: The one rule that protects you from all five: pay for travel with a credit card, through the airline, hotel or booking platform directly. Credit cards give you dispute rights if a booking turns out to be fake. Never pay for travel by wire, gift card, crypto or a payment app to a person.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a credit card with a shield No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wrap up
segments.narration: So reverse search, book direct, type the address, and pay by credit card. Save this before you book, send it to whoever's planning the trip, and follow for one scam decoded every day. Have a great spring break.

idea_angle: Job scams in 2027: reshipping and package jobs, fake checks for 'equipment', task and 'optimization' jobs that ask you to deposit money, and fake recruiters who want your ID. With the tells and what to do.

script.title: Job scams 2027: 4 fake jobs that cost you money (and how to spot them)
script.hook: 4 kinds of fake jobs are everywhere right now. Each 1 ends with you paying them.

segments.heading: Why now
segments.narration: Lots of people look for new jobs and side income in spring, and job scams follow. The FTC says job scams cost people a lot of money every year, and they're getting more convincing, with real-looking websites and friendly recruiters on messaging apps. Here are four fake jobs that all end the same way: with you paying them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding a job offer with a magnifier No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Reshipping
segments.narration: One, the reshipping job. 'Package inspector' or 'logistics coordinator', work from home. You receive packages, print labels they send you, and reship them. The goods are often bought with stolen cards, your address is on every box, and after a month the company disappears without paying you. Real companies don't run their logistics through employees' kitchens.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. boxes stacked at a kitchen table No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake checks
segments.narration: Two, the fake check job. You're hired as an assistant or remote worker, and they send you a check to buy 'equipment' from their approved vendor, or to pay other staff. You deposit it, send money on, and days later the check bounces. Now you owe your bank the whole amount. The FTC says that's how fake check scams work: the money's never really there.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a check bouncing like a ball No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Task jobs
segments.narration: Three, the task job. A recruiter messages you on a chat app: easy online work, rating products or 'optimizing' apps. You complete tasks on a website and see earnings pile up. Then you're told to deposit money, often crypto, to unlock the next set of tasks or withdraw your pay. The FTC calls these task scams. The earnings are fake, and every deposit is lost.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a game-like progress bar with a lock No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake recruiters
segments.narration: Four, the fake recruiter. They copy a real company's name and logo, interview you by text, and offer you the job quickly. Then they need your Social Security number, a photo of your driver's license and your bank details 'for onboarding'. That's identity theft. Real companies do collect some of this, but after a real interview and through their official HR systems.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an ID card being handed to a mask No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The 3 rules
segments.narration: Three rules protect any job search. One, you never pay to get or keep a job: no fees, no equipment checks, no deposits. Two, check the company yourself: find its official website and careers page, and contact HR through it. Three, be wary of jobs that come to you by text or chat app, with no real interview.
segments.on_screen_text: Never pay · check them · real interview
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. three check marks on a clipboard No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you've been hit
segments.narration: If you've already been hit: stop sending money, keep every message, contact your bank about any deposits or transfers, and report it at report fraud dot F T C dot gov. idea_angle: The last two weeks before the April tax deadline: how to file late safely, get a free extension, pay what you owe, and avoid the scams that target last-minute filers.

script.title: Filing last minute? How to beat the tax deadline safely (and the scams waiting for you)
script.hook: 2 weeks to the tax deadline. 5 scams target last-minute filers, and here's the safe way to finish.

segments.heading: Two weeks
segments.narration: The federal tax deadline is mid-April, so check IRS dot gov for this year's exact date. If you haven't filed yet, you're in good company, millions of people file in the last two weeks. But rushing is exactly what scammers count on. So here's the safe way to finish: filing, extensions, paying, and the five scams aimed at last-minute filers. General education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes with a calendar and a tax form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: File for free
segments.narration: First, filing. If your income is under the limit, IRS Free File lets you file with brand-name software for free. Start from I R S dot gov slash free file, not a search ad, because some ads lead to versions that charge. And VITA and TCE sites offer free in-person help for people who qualify, including many older adults. Find them on IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a laptop with a free sign No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Preparers
segments.narration: If you need a preparer fast, a few quick checks. Paid preparers must have a P T I N, a preparer tax ID, and must sign your return. Avoid anyone who bases their fee on the size of your refund, or wants the refund deposited into their account. And never sign a blank return.
segments.on_screen_text: Preparer: PTIN · signs · no refund cut
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a return with a signature line No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free extensions
segments.narration: If you can't finish in time, you can request an extension to file, for free, through IRS Free File or with Form forty-eight sixty-eight. Ignore anyone charging you just to file an extension. One important catch: an extension gives you more time to file, not more time to pay. If you owe, estimate and pay what you can by the deadline.
segments.on_screen_text: Extension: free, but pay by the deadline
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a calendar with an extended arrow No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paying
segments.narration: Paying safely: use I R S dot gov slash payments, typed yourself. You can pay directly from your bank account, by card through approved processors, or set up a payment plan if you can't pay in full. The IRS will never ask you to pay with gift cards, crypto, or a payment app to a person.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a laptop with a payments page No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The scams
segments.narration: Now the five scams. One, 'final notice, balance due' emails and texts with a pay link. Two, pop-up preparers who won't sign. Three, paid 'extension services' for something that's free. Four, search ads for 'free filing' that aren't free. Five, fake support numbers for tax software. The answer to all five is the same: start from I R S dot gov, or the software's own app.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. five warning signs in a row No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: After you file
segments.narration: After you file, keep a copy of your return and the records behind it. Check your refund status at I R S dot gov slash refunds. And for next year, get an IRS Identity Protection PIN, so nobody else can file in your name. Save this, send it to the last-minute filer in your family, and follow for one scam decoded every day.
